title: Just Show Me the Prompt
author: Leading in Product
summary: This Leading in Product piece diagnoses what its author calls 'document inflation': AI has made it effortless to generate long, polished-sounding text, and people are using that ease to pad documents that used to fit on one page into fifteen. The author's sharpest observation is a closed loop they call document laundering, where AI inflates a document on the writing end and AI compresses it again on the reading end, so no human ever actually engages with the real content or the thinking behind it. The deeper cost, the piece argues, is accountability: a long AI-generated document can disguise the fact that its author never thought deeply about the problem, because volume reads as effort even when it isn't. The practice the author has adopted with their own team is to ask for the prompt instead of the document, on the logic that a sharp, specific prompt reveals genuine understanding of a problem while a vague one reveals its absence, and that this question respects someone's time far more than skimming twenty pages does. The piece closes with concrete norms: default to one page, treat two pages as a deliberate choice, and ask for a one-page summary before committing time to anything longer.
points: The author names 'document laundering': AI inflates a document on the writing end while AI compresses it on the reading end, meaning no human ever fully engages with the actual content.
Length has become a false signal of effort and value, and the piece argues padding actively hides the fact that an author may never have thought deeply about the problem.
The core practice the author now uses with their team is asking to see the prompt instead of the document, treating the prompt as the 'truest artifact' of the person's actual thinking.
The recommended default is one page, with two pages requiring a deliberate choice, and a request for a one-page summary before investing time in anything longer.
quotes: AI has made it effortless to generate text. Beautiful, structured, confident-sounding text. And people are using that power generously. Too generously. Documents that could fit on one page now arrive as fifteen.
I now use AI to summarize the documents that others used AI to write. We have built a closed loop: a document laundering machine where AI inflates on one end and AI compresses on the other.
A long AI-generated document can hide the fact that the author never thought deeply about the problem at all. Length becomes a disguise, and a very convincing one.
If you used AI to write a document, your prompt is the truest artifact of your thinking. A sharp, specific prompt shows that you understood the problem. A vague prompt shows that you did not.
Asking for the prompt cuts straight to what matters, faster than reading twenty pages ever could. It is not rude. It is the most respectful thing you can do with someone's time.
Set expectations early. One page is almost always enough. Two pages should be a conscious choice. If someone sends you twenty pages, ask for a one-page summary before you invest your time.
